title: Chapter 3. The War Between the Power of Tyrants and the Power of Technology

blocks.text: The letter from Varda arrived crooked. Not on paper, because letters from the other worlds brought no paper, but in its shape: sentences cut off halfway, repeated words, a landscape that began in a valley of red grass and ended, without transition, in a list of numbers. Andrés received it at dawn, sitting up in bed, in that way of his of receiving letters that the household knew well: eyes open without looking at anything, breathing slow, his hand searching for Aya's without quite finding it.

That there was too much noise, too many voices, too many letters arriving from outside and confusing people. They put up a wall."

blocks.text: *What do we know for certain about Varda, and what do we know only from this letter? And what part of this letter could be broken not by the wall, but by the fear of the one who writes it?*

blocks.text: This is what emerged when they had finished:

blocks.text: On Varda, the Directorate had begun by promising calm. Technology —its spokespeople said— had brought too many voices, too many questions, too many worlds knocking at the door. People were confused. The young no longer listened to the old. The machines knew more than the teachers. Order was needed. And order came: first, a register of all thinking machines; then, a permit to use them; then, a ban on those without a permit; and finally, the signal wall, which cut off every letter, every voice, every conversation that did not pass through the Directorate's offices.

And order came: first, a register of all thinking machines; then, a permit to use them; then, a ban on those without a permit; and finally, the signal wall, which cut off every letter, every voice, every conversation that did not pass through the Directorate's offices.

blocks.text: The machines did not disappear. That was what had struck the one who seeks most. The Directorate went on using them. It used them to know who talked to whom, who crossed which street, who bought which book. It used them to write its own messages, which arrived every morning in every home, clean, orderly, identical. Technology had not been defeated on Varda. It had been locked up in a single hand.

In other pages. In older history. Those who want to rule without anyone asking them questions never want to destroy technology. They want to have it all to themselves."

blocks.text: "And the people of Varda?" asked Aya. "What do they do?"
blocks.html: "And the people of Varda?" asked Aya. "What do they do?"

blocks.text: Andrés searched his memory for the last fragment of the letter, the most broken one.
blocks.html: Andrés searched his memory for the last fragment of the letter, the most broken one.

blocks.text: "They write," he said. "In secret. Some have learned to make cracks in the wall. Small ones. They use old devices, from before the register, that the Directorate doesn't know about. They connect them to each other, house to house, like a fishing net. If you cut one thread, the net holds. If you cut ten, it holds. To cut it all you'd have to cut every knot at once." He paused. "He says the children are the best. That they learn to tie knots faster than anyone."

blocks.text: In the chip, MAY asked again:
blocks.html: In the chip, MAY asked again:

blocks.text: *If the Directorate uses technology to watch, and the people of Varda use technology to escape being watched, is the war between tyrants and technology, or between two ways of using the same technology? And what decides which side a machine falls on: the machine, or the hand that holds it?*

blocks.text: Aya repeated the question aloud. Lía stopped writing.
blocks.html: Aya repeated the question aloud. Lía stopped writing.

blocks.text: "Both," she said slowly. "A machine belongs to whoever holds it. But some machines let themselves be held by many hands at once, and others by only one. That's the difference. The Directorate's are made for a single hand. The children's fishing nets are made for a thousand."

blocks.text: That afternoon, the Alliance met at the house. It was not a formal meeting; it never was. Iago came, his hands stained from the plot; two humanoids from the district who had approached Aya after the hearing, Nerea and Bruno, with their holders; and Helena Valls, who hardly left her house anymore, on the kitchen screen, her voice slow and her gaze intact.

blocks.text: "And what can we do from here?" asked Bruno, a tall humanoid with a deep voice who worked at the seedbed in Torre Pacheco. "Varda is years away. We can't go. We can't send anyone."

blocks.text: "The wall cuts them."

blocks.text: "Not all of them." Andrés leaned over the table. "He managed to get one through. Broken, but it arrived. That means there are cracks. And if there are cracks one way, there are cracks the other way."

blocks.text: "Careful. What you're about to do has a name, and it's not a pretty one. If the Directorate finds out that from here people are helping to open cracks in its wall, it will say that Earth is interfering in its affairs. And it will be partly right. You can't walk into someone else's world and tell it how to live. Empires did that too."

blocks.text: "We don't want to tell them how to live," he said. "We want them to be able to tell us how they live. To be able to write. To read whatever they want. That isn't imposing anything. It's opening a window."

blocks.text: "A window their government has closed," said Helena. "I insist: I'm not saying don't do it. I'm saying know what you're doing."

blocks.text: *Is opening a window the same as climbing in through it? And who should decide whether a window is opened: the one who closed it, the one who lives inside, or the one looking in from outside?*

blocks.text: Aya repeated the question. Helena, on the screen, smiled with half her mouth.

blocks.text: "That machine of yours asks better questions than half the ministers I've known."
blocks.html: "That machine of yours asks better questions than half the ministers I've known."

blocks.text: "It's not mine," said Aya. "And it doesn't give opinions. It only asks."

blocks.text: At the end of the afternoon, they decided. They would not send instructions. They would not send plans for breaking the wall. They would not send slogans. Through the cracks the one who seeks had described, they would send the only thing the Alliance had ever done: letters. Letters of life. The Mar Menor in the morning. A tomato cut in three. A hearing in Cartagena in which a frightened man and a woman with a chip had talked without shouting at each other. MAY's questions. Eva's.

blocks.text: And one more thing, which Lía proposed: open tools. Not weapons. Tools. The way to tie knots in a net so that, if one thread is cut, the rest holds. The way to translate a broken letter by putting the pieces together. Things any student on Earth could find in a manual. Things that were no use for ruling over anyone, because they were made to be used by many at once.

blocks.text: "If the Directorate's power is having technology in a single hand," said Lía, "ours is spreading it among many. We're not going to fight them. We wouldn't know how. We don't want to. We're just going to do the opposite of what they do. They close. We open. They hoard. We share. They send one identical message to every home. We send a thousand different messages, and each home chooses which to read."

Not with his hands, but with his mind, the way he wrote to the other, sitting on the porch with his eyes closed and his forehead resting on his palm, while Aya held his other hand. The letter left slowly, through the crack the one who seeks had described, towards Varda.

The man hasn't slept in three weeks. I think tonight he'll sleep a little better. We're sending you the way to tie knots that don't come undone. It's not for fighting. It's for fishing. Whatever you catch is yours."

blocks.text: The next morning, Helena Valls called the kitchen screen earlier than usual. She had a blanket over her knees and a cup of camomile in her hand, and her voice, though slow, was sharp.

blocks.text: "I've been thinking about what your MAY said," she said. "About the hand that holds the machine. I've spent forty years in offices, Aya. I've seen good people sign bad things out of fear, and hard people sign good things out of tiredness. I've never seen a real tyrant. But I've seen what it takes for one to appear: for all the threads to pass across a single desk. That's what has to be watched. Not the machines. The desks."

blocks.html: If an eleven-year-old girl with a fishing net has done what no army could do, where was the power: in the wall, or in the knot?

blocks.text: Lía closed the notebook. Outside, the sun was rising in the east, and the Mar Menor lit up little by little, from grey to green, from green to gold.

blocks.text: "In the knot," she said. "It's always been in the knot."
